cards.explanation: The reason God gives is that the LORD their God is holy. He says, “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy.” (Leviticus 19:2) God doesn't point to a rule or a crowd. He points to who He is. And He says it to the whole congregation of Israel, so nobody gets to sit this one out.

The word is mother. God says each person “…must respect his mother and father…” (Leviticus 19:3) Both parents get named, so neither one gets skipped. That's a good place to start holy living, right at the kitchen table.

The answer is True, friends. God says, “Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves molten gods.” (Leviticus 19:4) That's two things: don't turn to idols, and don't make molten gods. Then He signs it the way He signed the last command: “I am the LORD your God.”

What's left of the peace offering on the third day must be burned up. “…what remains on the third day must be burned up.” (Leviticus 19:6) The offering gets two days to be eaten, the day you sacrifice it or the next. After that, there's no day three for the leftovers. The next verse says if any of it is eaten on the third day, it “…is tainted and will not be accepted.” (Leviticus 19:7)

The answer is False. The verse says, “If any of it is eaten on the third day, it is tainted and will not be accepted.” (Leviticus 19:7) Tainted and not accepted, that's how plainly God puts it. So the third-day rule is no small thing.

God says to leave them for the poor and the foreigner. “Leave them for the poor and the foreigner.” (Leviticus 19:10) The same goes for the edges of the field and the gleanings from verse 9. So God has the harvest leave something on the table for people who need it. And He signs it, “I am the LORD your God.”

The word is profane, friends. “You must not swear falsely by My name and so profane the name of your God.” (Leviticus 19:12) Swearing falsely drags God's own name into a lie. And God closes it with “I am the LORD…”

The hired hand must be paid before the next morning. “You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand.” (Leviticus 19:13) The pay is due before morning comes. That's a short deadline, friends. Payday doesn't get to hit the snooze button.

The answer is False. God says, “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God.” (Leviticus 19:14) There's no clause tucked in there about not being able to tell who did it. The command stands as written, and it ends with “I am the LORD…”

The answer is False. The verse says, “you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly.” (Leviticus 19:15) The scale doesn't tip toward either side. A neighbor is a neighbor, and each one gets a fair hearing.

The answer is True. “You must not go about spreading slander among your people.” (Leviticus 19:16) The command is about going around with it among your own people. The same verse adds, “You must not endanger the life of your neighbor.” Then it closes with “I am the LORD…”

God tells Israel to rebuke their neighbor directly. “Directly rebuke your neighbor…” (Leviticus 19:17) It comes right after “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart.” So instead of keeping it inside, God says to rebuke your neighbor directly. The word is directly, friends.

God says to rebuke your neighbor directly so that you won't incur guilt on account of him. “Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him.” (Leviticus 19:17) That's the reason God gives, and it's the only one in the verse. It comes right after the command not to harbor hatred in your heart. I think it shows how seriously He takes the way people treat each other.

God calls for them to love their neighbor as themselves. “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.” (Leviticus 19:18) Notice the word but. God doesn't stop at telling them what to drop. He tells them what to pick up instead.

The answer is False. The verse says, “…you shall not wear clothing made of two kinds of material.” (Leviticus 19:19) It comes right after the two kinds of livestock and the two kinds of seed. The text doesn't say why, so I'll leave it right where God put it.

In the fourth year, the fruit is offered to the LORD in praise. “In the fourth year all its fruit must be consecrated as a praise offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 19:24) Three years it's forbidden, and then in year four, all of it is offered to Him in praise. All of it, not just some. The eating for Israel comes in the fifth year. (Leviticus 19:25)

The answer is True. “But in the fifth year you may eat its fruit; thus your harvest will be increased.” (Leviticus 19:25) That comes after three forbidden years and a praise offering in year four. Then God signs it, “I am the LORD your God.” So the long wait comes with an increase attached.

They will be defiled by them. “You must not turn to mediums or spiritists; do not seek them out, or you will be defiled by them.” (Leviticus 19:31) There are two commands in there: don't turn to them, and don't seek them out. The result God names is being defiled by them. And He closes it with “I am the LORD your God.”

God tells Israel to rise and honor the elderly. “You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God. I am the LORD.” (Leviticus 19:32) When an older person walks in, you stand up. Then you honor them. And God puts fearing Him right in the same verse.

Israel should treat the foreigner as one of their native-born. “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born…” (Leviticus 19:34) Not a second-class guest, but one of their own. The verse goes on, “…and love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” So God doesn't just say to tolerate him, He says to love him.

The reason God gives is that they were foreigners in Egypt. “…love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.” (Leviticus 19:34) So Israel knows from their own history what it's like to be the outsider. God points them right back to that.

The word is scales, friends. “You shall maintain honest scales and weights, an honest ephah, and an honest hin.” (Leviticus 19:36) An ephah and a hin are both measures, one for dry goods and one for liquid. And God signs it with “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”
